text:
Verses 1-15

In the name of God, the most Merciful, the most Compassionate The purpose of the chapter (sūrah) is to warn and give glad tidings. This is evidenced by the chapter’s concluding verses where God says: So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good news thereby to those who guard (against evil) and warn thereby a vehemently contentious people (19:97).

This objective is achieved in an innovative approach that begins by recounting the stories of Zachariah and John [the Baptist], Mary and Jesus, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses and Aaron, Ishmael (Ismāʿīl) and Enoch (Idrīs) [peace be upon them all]. It describes that which was conferred to them of the favor (niʿmah) of divine guardianship (wilāyāh) such as Prophethood, truthfulness and purity of action. It then retells that these individuals, whom God favored, were known for their submission and humility to their Lord. Regrettably, the verses continue, they were succeeded by those that turned away from that path by becoming heedless to their Lord, following their base desires instead. In turn, they will

ultimately meet their perdition and loose their rectitude. Only those of them that repent and return to their Lord will be joined with the people of divine favor (niʿmah).

The chapter then discusses selections of the blunders and delusions that the people of error fall into including (1) their denial of Hereafter, (2) their belief that “God has taken a son to Himself” [vide 19:88] and (3) their worship of idols. It then continues by depicting the punishment and retribution that they will face as a consequence of these devastating mistakes.

Hence, the discourse in this chapter can best be compared with that of a prosecutor making his case by citing legal precedents. It is as if the chapter is saying: The approach of so-and-so and so-and-so, who were on the path of rectitude and were blessed by God, was to abstain from base desires, and to turn toward their Lord. Their custom was to be submissive and humble whenever the communications of their Lord were recited to them. This is mankind’s approach to rectitude and divine favor (niʿmah). On the other hand, those who came after them abandoned this approach by turning away from righteous deeds toward reprehensible desires. This only led them to perdition as opposed to rectitude. Further, it only settled them in false beliefs such as denying the return to God and affirming partners for Him. It only drove them to obstruct the call to God and only led them into divine retribution and chastisement.

Therefore, as the reader can see, the chapter begins by providing examples to then deduce the universal lesson to be illustrated. A prime example

is found in the verse: These are they on whom God bestowed favors …(19:58) The chapter classifies people into three groups, namely (1) the top beneficiaries of God’s favors, including the Prophets, the chosen ones and the people of guidance, (2) those people of error and perdition and (3) those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds, who will be joined with the people of God’s favor (niʿmah) and of rectitude, the top benef ciaries of God’s favors.

The chapter then discusses the reward of those who repent and seek rectitude, as well as the punishment of those in perdition. It describes the latter group as the peers and loyal associates of the devils.

This chapter was revealed in Mecca without a doubt, as shown and verified by the content of the verses and by the consensus of the exegetes.

(19:1) KāfiHāʾ Yāʾ ʿAyn Ṣād

At the beginning of the exegesis of Sūrah al-ʾAʿrāf, it was mentioned [in Ar. vol. 8] that the chapters which begin with a combination of disjoint alphabetical letters (ḥūrūf-muqaṭṭaʿah) are thematically linked to

these opening letters. Hence, chapters that share the same opening letters will also contain common themes. This is supported by some of the links and similarities seen between this chapter and Sūrah Ṣād, [especially in] regard to telling the stories of the Prophets. There will be a comprehensive discussion later on, God willing, on the links between the disjoint opening letters and the contents of the chapters which begin with them. In turn, a comparative analysis on the themes of chapters that share the same opening letters is in order. For example, we will compare this chapter and Sūrah Yā Sīn, insofar as they have the letter yāʾ in common, and this chapter and Sūrah al-Shūrā [The Counsel], insofar as they have the letter ʿayn in common.

(19:2) A mention (dhikr) of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zachariah.

It is apparent from the context that ‘mention’ (dhikr) is the predicate of an implied subject. The verbal noun (that is, dhikr) is the same as the object. The implied meaning is: “This is a communication of your Lord’s aforementioned (madhkūr) mercy”. The ‘aforementioned mercy’ is God’s answer to Zachariah’s prayer, the details of which are in the story He immediately tells in the coming verses. This is evidenced by what He says subsequently: When he called upon his Lord in a low voice.

(19:3) When (idh) he called upon his Lord in a low voice.

The locative object (ẓarf) [idh meaning “when”] is connected to the “mercy of your Lord”. The words nidāʾ and munādāt both mean calling out loud. It is not contradictory to describe it as hidden (khafiyy) because it is possible to loudly call out in private without people hearing one’s call.

This is also the impression given by: “So he came out to his people from his place of worship”. [19:11]

Some exegetes have said that the point of using the word nidāʾ is to convey the fact that he considered himself to be distanced from God due to his sins and poor circumstances, as is the condition of one who fears His punishment.

(19:4) He said: My Lord! surely my bones are weakened and my head fiares with gray, and, my Lord! I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You.

This opens the prelude to what he [Zachariah] is going to ask for: therefore grant me from Yourself an heir. He put the word rabbī (my Lord) first, at the beginning of the supplication, to seek and plead for divine mercy (raḥmah). The expression innā which contains inna, meaning ‘surely’, further affirms Zachariah’s oneness with his total need [to God]. Wahn means weakness and deficiency in strength. He attributed this weakness to al-ʿaẓm (the bone) because it is the substructure that supports the body in motion and at rest. He did not say al-ʿiẓam minnī (these bones of mine) or ʿaẓmī (my bones). Instead, he referred to ‘bones’ by genus, pointing to the intrinsic characteristics of all bones. Hence, he stated that which applies generally before that which pertains particularly to himself. And my head fiares with gray:ʾIshtiʿal means the spread of a fire’s flames and blaze in something which is burning. Majmaʿ al-bayān says: “Wa [i]shtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban is one of the most beautiful metaphors. It means that gray or white hair fiared and spread around the head like a fire’s diffusion”. Here the intending meaning of diffusion (shuʿāʿ) is a fire’s

flames and blaze.

Shaqāwa which means misery is the opposite of saʿāda which means felicity. It means being deprived of good, which is concomitant to misery or is synonymous with it. Bi duʿaʾika, in my supplication to You, is linked to shaqiyyan, miserable. The letter bāʾ indicates causation (because of). Alternatively, it means f (in). All together, it means: “I was fortunate because of my supplication to You. Every time I pray to You, You answer me without rendering me miserable”. Another alternative is: “I have never been deprived and disappointed in my supplication to You. You have made me accustomed to Your response whenever I call You and to Your acceptance whenever I petition You”. In any event the word duʿāʾ, supplication,

is a verbal noun (maṣdar) annexed to the object.

Some exegetes have said in the alternative that bi duʿāʾika is a verbal noun annexed to the subject, meaning: “I have never been wretched, rebellious, or disobedient to Your call to servitude and obedience, but rather I

am servile to You and sincere in obedience to You”. However, the previous interpretation is more likely.

There is eloquence beyond measure in repeating the word rabbī (my Lord) and positioning it between the subject and predicate of the verb kān (was) in: akun (first person singular jussive form of the verb implying the subject) bi duʿāʾika rabbī shaqiyyan (predicate) (and, my Lord! I

have never been wretched in my supplication to You). Wa [i]jʿalhu rabbī raḍiyyan (and make him, my Lord, one in whom You are well pleased) is sim ilar to it.

(19:5) And surely I fear my paternal uncles and and their sons (mawālī) after me, and my wife was barren … This completes the prelude to Zachariah’s plea to God to grant him an heir from Himself. Mawālī here means paternal uncles and their sons. Other interpretations for mawālī that exegetes have adopted include (1) indirect heirs other than father or son relations (kalālah), (2) direct or indirect male heirs (ʿuṣbah), (3) the sons of paternal uncles exclusively and (4) heirs in general. Irrespective, it is clear that mawālī refers to heirs other

than one’s biological children. Hence the intended meaning is: “I fear the doing of the mawālī after me, meaning, after my death”. He feared that he would die without children as heirs to inherit from him. Hence, mawālī was used as a metonymy to express the consequence that Zachariah feared: to die without anyone to carry after him [from his loins].

… and my wife was barren: A woman who is ʿāqir is one that cannot bear children while a man who is ʿāqir cannot beget any children. Hence, when he said: and my wife was barren, he, first, implied that she was barren and, secondly, that she has passed the childbearing age at the time

of his supplication. The ability of this verse to be so concise and clear of repetition is due to (1) the fact that, and my wife was barren is a circumstantial phrase and (2) the segment of the verse from, and surely I fear till

was barren is a single atomic unit. As a result, this segment of the verse could read as: “My wife’s barrenness dictates that I should fear my paternal uncles and their sons (mawālī) after I have passed away”.

Everything Zachariah said in prelude [, in verses 4 and 5,] to the heart of his supplication [, starting from “therefore grant from Yourself an heir” till the end of verse 6,] can be broken down into two parts. The first part is that God had answered his supplications time and again throughout his life, until he had become old and feeble. The second part is that he feared his paternal uncles and their sons after his death because of his wife’s barrenness. It is also reasonable to look at the words as comprised of three parts, taking the descriptions of his old age and his wife barrenness as two distinct parts.

(19:5-6) … therefore grant me from Yourself an heir, Who should inherit from me and inherit from the children of Jacob, and make him, my Lord, pleasing.

This is the actual core of Zachariah’s supplication. The conditional clause “from Yourself” applied to “grant me” expresses Zachariah’s despair from the ordinary means at his disposal, himself having become old and decrepit and having lost his strength and his wife having become old having previously been barren.

A person’s waliyy is someone who takes charge of his affairs. The waliyy of the deceased is someone who takes care of his affairs and inherits his estate. A man’s family (āl) is his elect and closest, [those] whom he

is responsible for, example, his children, relatives, and companions. It is said that its etymological origin is ahl. Jacob, as some have said, means Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham. Alternatively, it is said that it means, Jacob son of Māthān, brother of of Amram son of Māthān. Amram son of Māthān is Mary’s father and Zachariah’s wife was Mary’s sister. Hence, based on this interpretation, who should inherit from me and inherit from the children of Jacob means: “who should inherit from me and inherit from my wife who is a relative to Jacob’s family”. On the basis of this interpretation, the most likely grammatical explanation of min in min Āl Yaʿqūb

is that it is partitive meaning “of Jacob’s family”, even though it would also be correct to interpret it as a locative meaning “from Jacob’s family”. In the phrase, and make him, my Lord, pleasing (raḍiyyan), raḍiyy means marḍiyy, that is, with whom God is well pleased. The lack of any specificity to raḍiyy broadens the scope of its applicability to include knowledge and deeds. Thus it depicts one whose belief and deeds are well-pleasing to God. All together it means: “My Lord, grace him with useful knowledge and good deeds”.

God told this story at the end of the account of Mary in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān [The Family of Amram] which is Medinite—that is, revealed after [Sūrah] Mary, which is Meccan: … So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and made her grow up a good growing, and gave her into the charge of Zachariah; whenever Zachariah entered the sanctuary to (see) her, he found with her food. He said: O Mary! whence comes this to you? She said: It is from God. Surely God gives to whom He pleases without measure He said: O Mary! whence comes this to you? She said: It is from God. Surely God gives to whom He pleases without measure.There did Zachariah pray to his Lord; he said: My Lord! grant me from You good offspring; surely You are the Hearer of supplication (3:35-38).

Anyone reflecting on the above two verses should not be in any doubt that what led Zachariah to supplicate as he did, in verses 4 to 6, was seeing how Mary was esteemed in the sight of God by virtue of her servitude and sincerity of deeds. This sparked in Zachariah the desire to beseech God to grant him offspring as favored and esteemed before Him as was Mary. Then, he complained to God about his old age and infirmity and about the old age and barrenness which had befallen his wife. More so, he continued that his indirect heirs, his paternal uncles and their sons, did not have the aptitude to carry after him and the prospect of their indirect successorship grieved him. Notwithstanding, he was mindful and certain that his Lord repeatedly answered his supplications and sufficed him in every matter. Thus he sought refuge in his Lord, supplicating and evoking God to grant him a good offspring.

The divine words in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān: My Lord! grant me from You good offspring equates with the words in Sūrah Maryam: therefore grant me from Yourself an heir who should inherit from me and inherit from the children of Jacob, and make him, my Lord, pleasing.

The word “good” (ṭayyibah) [, in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān] equates with the words “and make him, my Lord, pleasing (raḍiyyan)”. The intent of Zachariah when he supplicated for an offspring that would be wellpleasing was that they would have favor and esteem with God like he witnessed in Mary by virtue of her good deeds. In turn, My Lord! grant me

from You offspring equates and explains, therefore grant me from Yourself an heir, who should inherit from me and inherit from the children of Jacob. Hence, an heir, who should inherit from me speaks of an heir directly from his offspring.

With this understanding, the incorrectness of the following claims becomes clear including those that said (1) that, therefore grant me from Yourself an heir, who should inherit from me means that he was asking for someone to take his place, irrespective of whether he was a son or not, or (2) that He despaired of having a child with his wife so he asked for his successorship and role to be passed on to anyone deemed worthy, be he from any of his people. Furthermore, using the words, therefore grant me (hab lī) is suggestive of a type of ownership which cannot properly be said of anyone who is not a member of his family. Such non-familial relationships are best described with the expression jaʿl, making, as found in: … and give us (wa ajʿal lanā) from You a guardian and give us (wa ajʿal lanā) from You a helper (4:75).

Thus it is clear that, an heir (waliyy), who should inherit from me means offspring as it is referred to in the verse in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān by the term dhurriyya which means offspring. Hence, here waliyy (heir) equates with dhurriyya (offspring) and it is the custodian (waliyy) of one’s inheritance. Further, the inheritance in question is that of the inheritance of the estate of the deceased including their wealth and material assets. No matter how we conceive of inheritance, without a doubt, material inheritance always comes to mind. On one hand, if we think of inheritance as literally implying the inheritance of wealth and property all while implying metaphorically the inheritance of immaterial possessions or attributes such

as knowledge, then our conception of inheritance includes the material dimension. On the other hand, if we take inheritance to literally imply all aspects of inheritance, including the material and the immaterial, then our understanding of inheritance also includes the material. In any event, the apparent and most immediate meaning of the expression, yarithunī—who should inherit from me, is the inheritance of wealth and property. Hence, the intent in qualifying waliyy, which generally means guardian or custodian, with yarithunī, meaning who should inherit from me, is to denote

a child or a biological heir. Moreover, the preceding phrase, and surely I fear my paternal uncles and their sons after me, serves to increase the likelihood of an heir (waliyy), who should inherit from me meaning material

inheritance. Further explanation of this is coming up, God willing. The claim that, therefore grant me from Yourself an heir, who should inherit from me means inheritance of Prophethood and that he asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit his Prophethood is refuted by what the reader has already learned. Zachariah’s incentive to supplicate and make his request before God was what he witnessed in Mary. There is no oral tradition or evidence for her having been a Prophetess. Hence, what link is there between his being impressed with her worship and her honor in the sight of God, and his asking his Lord for a son to inherit his Prophethood? Moreover, Prophethood is not obviously hereditary. Even if we accept, for the sake of argument that inheritance here just means one Prophet coming after another or that a Prophet comes from the offspring of another through a kind of divine care, another problem would arise. Namely, based on this interpretation, it would be inappropriate to say subsequently: and make him, my Lord, pleasing. This is because it makes no sense to say: “Grant me a son who is a Prophet and make him one in whom You are well pleased”. If it is construed as emphasis, it emphasizes something of a higher rank like Prophethood through something of a lower rank such as being well-pleasing.

A logical inconsistency also emerges in interpreting raḍiyy as pleasing to people because it opposes the broadness of applicability of the

expression raḍiyy, as discussed above. This is in addition to the fact that this interpretation does not match the reason he had for saying this supplication as mentioned earlier.1

Almost as incorrect as the above interpretation is the claim that inheritance in, therefore grant me from Yourself an heir means inheritance of

knowledge. In other words, he asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit his knowledge. There is no causal link between Zachariah being impressed with Mary’s worship and spiritual rank and his asking his Lord for a son to inherit his knowledge.

Other exegetes have said that inheritance means inheritance of knowledge and that, And make him, my Lord, pleasing, refers to good deeds.

Beneficial knowledge and good deeds together, they continued, is the like of what he saw in Mary’s sincerity, her worship, and her status with God. However, this is refuted by the fact that the clause, and make him, my Lord, pleasing (raḍiyy), alone suffices to recount that Zachariah evoked God to be granted a son that held beneficial knowledge and performed good deeds. As explained earlier, raḍiyy, is a standalone unbounded qualifier and encompasses both knowledge and deeds. However, if we accept

the interpretation that well-pleasing describes a person who performs good deeds with little attention to knowledge, we contradict the premise

1 That is, seeing Mary’s characteristics. See above (Trans.)

that well-pleasing (marḍiyy) meant pleasing in every way. Similarly, the claim that raḍiyy means pleasing to the people also does not align with the expression’s broadness by restricting its application to one aspect without another.

Almost as incorrect is the claim that inheritance means the inheritance of piety (taqwā) and esteem and that he asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit his [Zachariah’s] closeness to God and his station in His sight. Author’s comment: It would have been appropriate for him in the context shown earlier with the related verses from Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān, to ask for

a son as close and esteemed to God as was Mary, or simply to ask for a son that is close and esteemed in the absolute sense, and not to ask for a son to whom his own closeness and rank with God would pass. Furthermore, it does not fit with what he said, “And surely I fear my paternal uncles and their sons after me” because it is apparent from the context that he was asking for a son to inherit from him and to whom everything—that would otherwise pass to his indirect heirs (mawālī)—could pass. He feared that they would exploit that after his death. Of course, there is no reason to believe that he feared that his indirect heirs (mawālī) would gain proximity and rank with God and that they become God wary and noble, either

before his death or after. Prophets stand aloof of any such miserliness. Their sole wish is nothing but the well-being and felicity of all people. Some claim that his indirect heirs (mawālī) were the worst of the Children of Israel, so he feared that they would not be good successors to him in his nation after his death.

Author’s comment: If this succession means divine esoteric spiritual succession, it is definitely not hereditary. More so, it never misses its

rightful target and can only ever be assumed by its true owner. There is no reason to fear for it. If it means a worldly exoteric material succession, which is passed down through one’s line or by similar means, it is then a societal acquisition and one of the chattels of life in this world—like property. Thus, there is no point in not interpreting the inheritance in the verse as inheritance of property and instead interpreting it as inheritance of succession and government.

Furthermore, John did not take [charge of] any of the caliphate or government, which would have indicated that [he saw it] as his inheritance and was thus depriving his father’s kinsmen from inheriting it, nor did the Children of Israel have any dominion during the time of Zachariah or John. On the contrary, they were under Roman occupation and rule. Some exegetes have said that the interpretation of inheritance in the verse refers to the inheritance of knowledge and so on, not property. They explain that this is supported by the fact that there is not even a fly’s wingspan’s inclination toward worldly chattels in the high outlooks and highest

aspirations possessed by holy souls—especially Zachariah’s—which have cut themselves offfrom attachments to this fieeting, ephemeral world, and instead cling to the everlasting world. Zachariah was well-known for being completely cut offand detached, so ordinarily it would be impossible for him to worry, show concern, sorrow or fear on account of the

inheritance of money and chattels which by his high standards did not have the slightest value. Saying that he made a supplication like this to his Lord for such motives would falsely imply that his heart was completely attached and in love with this world and its embellishments. Further, they continue, that saying that he asked his Lord for a pleasing heir because he feared his kinsmen would spend his money on what they should not after his death also lacks evidence. They elaborate that when a man dies and his property passes through inheritance to another, it becomes the property of the beneficiary. From there, spending it is the beneficiary’s responsibility irrespective of whether he does so properly or wrongly, and there is no censure or blame on the deceased. Further, they go on, dispelling this fear would have been easy for him, as he could have disposed of

all his money before his death, and given it all to charity on God’s path, [thereby] leaving his evil paternal cousins disappointed because of their bad ways and repugnant deeds. Hence, they conclude, his only motive for asking for a son was to apply God’s laws, spread the Shariah, and for Prophethood to continue in his offspring.

Author’s comment: The objection presented above is based on the belief that [his supplication], grant me from Yourself an heir, who should inherit from me, is a request for his offspring to inherit his property, when in fact the opposite is true. His primary motive behind saying, an heir, who should inherit me, was to ask for a son, as is also clear from the direct speech cited: … My Lord! grant me from You good offspring, and elsewhere

(3:38), … O my Lord leave me not alone (21:89).

The clause, who should inherit from me, is just a contextual indication that waliyy here means heir, that is, son because the word, wilāyah

(guardianship), has a general meaning applicable in different ways. The only way the specific meaning of wilāyah can be disambiguated is with a contextual identifier. For example, in: … and they shall have no friends (awliyāʾ) to help them besides God (42:46), the guardianship (wilāyah) is qualified as being a guardianship of help and support. Another example is in: … and (as for) the believing men and the believing women, they are guardians (awliyāʾ) of each other; they enjoin good and forbid evil (9:71). Here wilāya means upholding societal balance because it is qualified by enjoining good and forbidding evil. There are other examples.

With this understanding, it becomes clear that if there had been no indication of financial inheritance to designate the nature of the guardianship (wilāyat) in question, there would be nothing lefiito indicate that

a son is being asked for, which was the very purpose of the supplication. Inheritance of knowledge, Prophethood, worship, and spiritual status do not signify that an inheritor is [necessarily] a son, as confirmed by exegetes that understood the verse to refer to inheritance of one of these kinds. Without a qualifier to the type of guardian (waliyy) being asked for, the supplication is rendered empty of its desired intent. This response is sufficient to render the above argument without foundation.

In summary, the true purport of his request is that he wanted a son. He did not really want an heir to his “fortune”. That was just a contextual clue that what he really meant by heir was a son. True, by the fact itself, it indicates that if he had a son he would inherit his property. Even so, in the expression, an heir, who should inherit me, or likewise in his words, and surely I fear my paternal uncles and cousins after me, there is no indication of his heart being attached to the temporal world or to its deceptive

embellishments.

As for asking for a son, it is part of the instinct which God has placed in the entire human race good and bad, Prophet and non-Prophet alike. He equipped everyone with a procreative system and placed in everyone the instinct to procreate. Everyone, provided his instinct has not deviated, is drawn toward trying to have children. He sees the survival of his child after his own death as a survival of himself and their taking possession of the necessities of life which he had been in possession of—inheritance—as his own possession and own livelihood.

The divine codes of law did not repeal this instinctive law or criticize this instinctive drive. On the contrary, they praise it and encourage it. There are many verses in the noble Qur’an that indicate this, for example, quoting Abraham: My Lord! grant me of the doers of good deeds (37:100); Praise be to God, who has given me in old age Ishmael [Ismāʿīl] and Isaac [Isḥāq]; most surely my Lord is the Hearer of supplication (14:39), and, quoting the believers: … O our Lord! grant us in our wives and our offspring the

joy of our eyes … (25:74) There are other similar verses.

You may say that the above explanation of the meaning of inheritance was based on an inference from “There did Zachariah pray to his Lord”

(3:38), that what made him ask for a child was seeing Mary’s worship and spiritual rank. He then wanted to be blessed with a child who could equal her in worship and spiritual status. However, it is also possible that his motivation was something else. Some oral traditions say that Zachariah would find fruits out of season around Mary—winter fruits in summer and summer fruits in winter. He then said to himself: If it is not difficult for God to provide winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter, then it would not be difficult for him to provide me with a child “out of season”—my being old and my wife being barren. Thereafter, he said: … therefore grant me from Yourself an heir, who should inherit from me. Thus, seeing fruit out of season made him ask for a child “out of season”. However, this noble Prophet was too honorable to ask for a child to inherit his property. He only asked for one to inherit Prophethood or knowledge or worship and rank in the sight of God.

Author’s comment: There is no evidence in the wording of (3:37) that rizq, meaning sustenance, specifically means fruit out of season and that what made Zachariah ask for a child was either witnessing that or Mary’s telling him, Surely God gives to whom He pleases without measure. If it were the case that it was Zachariah’s motivation, it would have been alluded to more clearly. Rather, what is conveyed from the apparent, from the context, especially the beginning of the verse (3:37)—“So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and made her grow well”1—is that Mary was had reached such a high rank with her Lord that He provided for her in a manner than transcended natural means. This spiritual rank was the real motive that inspired Zachariah to ask for good offspring and a son with whom God would be well pleased.

If that is conceded, what it means is that Zachariah was provoked first

1 God accepted her offering graciously and caused her to grow up admirably (Tarif

Khalidi’s translation) (Ed.)

into asking for offspring—a son. Since he was a noble Prophet he had no desire to have anything other than a good son, so he prayed, secondly, for him to be good and one in whom God would be well pleased. This is evidenced by the remainder of his supplication by saying: … and make him, my Lord, one in whom You are well pleased and qualifying him as “good” in “good offspring”.

He said what he meant, according to his direct speech attributed to him in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān … grant me from You good offspring, and in this chapter—after first making reference to his old age, his wife’s barrenness and his fear of his kinsmen, he said, … therefore grant me from Yourself an heir, who should inherit from me. Here, An heir who should inherit from me, means a son, without a doubt. He just referred to by giving it the title of guardianship in inheritance (wilāyah al-ʾirth). Guardianship in inheritance (wilāyah al-ʾirth), which can always be taken as a qualifier for a son,

is the guardianship that exclusively entitles him to the inheritance of what has been lefiibehind by the deceased parent.

As for (1) guardianship in inheritance of Prophethood—if it is correct to refer to it as inheritance, (2) guardianship in inheritance of knowledge, where the student inherits his teacher’s knowledge, and (3) guardianship in inheritance of esoteric rank and spiritual status, all of these are independent of lineage. At times they are accompanied with familial ties and

at times they are not. Hence, each of these types of ‘inheritances’ cannot be used to infer lineage or birthright without strong evidence. However, there nothing in the wording of the verse that can provide convincing clues. Whatever may be deemed fit to make a case can also be used to show the opposite. As a result, holding on the idea that the inheritance refers to one of Prophethood, knowledge or spiritual rank is tantamount to leaving the primary and immediately meaning to busy oneself with what could be behind it. That alone should suffice as a refutation of the claim.

(19:7) O Zachariah! surely We give you good news of a boy whose name shall be John. We have not made before anyone his equal.

There is an omission for the sake of brevity in the sentence, O Zachariah! surely We give you good news of a boy whose name shall be John. The implied meaning is, so We answered him and called to him: O Zachariah! Surely We give you good news of a boy whose name shall be John.

Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ [The Prophets] says: So We responded to him and gave him John (21:90). Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān [The Family of Amram] says: Then the Angels called to him as he stood praying in the sanctuary: That God gives you the good news of John (3:39).

The verse in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān is evidence that, O Zachariah! surely We give you good news … was revealed through the Angels, that is, His Words were passed on by the Angels to Zachariah. It is clearer in the second statement: He said: So shall it be, your Lord says: It is easy for Me (19:9). There is

an indication in the verse that it was God who named John—whose name shall be John (Yaḥyā)—and that no one before him had been given this name: We have not made before anyone (samiyyā), that is, anyone who shares the same name. It would not be surprising if samiyy meant equal to him as outlined below, that is, so serve Him and be patient in His service: Do you know anyone equal to Him (samiyyā) … (19:65). Further testimony to this is the fact that God conferred upon him epithets accorded to none of His Prophets and friends before him, for example: … and We granted him wisdom while yet a child (19:12); … and honorable and chaste (3:39); And peace on him on the day he was born, and on the day he dies, and on the day he is raised to life (19:15).

Even though, his maternal cousin, the Messiah, shared some of these epithets except that he was born after John.

(19:8) He said: O my Lord! when shall I have a son (ghulām), and my wife is barren, and I myself have reached indeed the extreme degree of old age:

Al-Rāghib says:

A ghulām is one who has begun to grow a mustache. Alternatively, it is said that a ghulām refers to a human male in the period between birth to the age of seventeen. He said [quoting Zachariah]: when shall I have a son (ghulām). In Arabic the verb ightalama means he reached the age of puberty.

Majmaʿ al-bayān says:

Al-ʿatiyy and al-ʿaṣiyy mean the same thing. Third person perfect tense: ʿatā; third person present tense: yaʿtū; absolute object: ʿutuwwan or ʿatiyyan. Third person perfect tense: ʿaṣā; third person present tense: yaʿṣū; absolute object: ʿuṣuwwan or ʿaṣiyyan.

Someone is said to be ʿātin or ʿāṣin if time has turned them dry. Reaching the age of al-ʿatiyy is an allusion to the loss of libido and an end to the means of procreation.

Zachariah’s question about the birth of a son despite his wife’s barrenness and his own extreme old age, notwithstanding his own reference to

both matters in his supplication, My Lord! surely my bones are weakened …, stems from his astonishment at these glad tidings and his desire for clarification of its particularity. It is not an indication that he considered it to be unlikely, nor is it a denial of it. Someone who is given good news of something which is unexpected because of there being impediments and the lack of means to achieve it becomes restless when he first hears it. He starts asking about the particulars of what he has been given good news about to put his heart at rest and to calm the disturbance within his soul. In spite of that, he is certain of the truthfulness of what he has been given good news of. Indeed, passing thoughts may not stop in spite of one’s knowledge and firm belief. Something similar was said by way of exegesis (in Eng. vol. 2) of: And when Abraham said: My Lord! show me how You give life to the dead, He said: What! and do you not believe? He said: Yes, but that my heart may be at ease (2:260).

(19:9) He said: So shall it be, your Lord says: It is easy for Me, and indeed I created you before, when you were nothing.

This is an answer to what he asked and sought clarification on to put his soul at rest and calm his heart. The pronoun in “He said” refers to God and kadhālik (lit. “like that”) is a direct speech quotation. It is the predicate of an implied subject. The implied meaning is: “It is like that, that is, the matter will come to pass as We have told you of it in the good news. There is no doubt about it”.

The words, your Lord says: It is easy for Me, and indeed I created you before, when you were nothing, are a second direct speech quotation introduced by the initial “He said”. It is like an explanation for kadhālik (like

that). All amazement is dispelled because His will does not fail to happen: His command, when He intends anything, is only to say to it: Be, so

it is (36:82).

Thus, creating a boy from a man who had reached old age and a woman who was barren was easy for Him.

In the same story, as told in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān, the question and answer are worded as: He said: My Lord! when shall there be a son (born) to me, and old age has already come upon me, and my wife is barren? He said: even thus God does what He pleases (3:40).

Thus, It is easy for Me, parallels, does God what He pleases. It supports the interpretation presented above. Further, and indeed I created you before, when you were nothing, gives an example of creation which clears up any astonishment.

Other explanations have been given for the verse, none of which are supported by the context, including:

1) Kadhālik is linked to the second “said” (qāl). The sentence put all together is the response. It means: Your Lord ordered that and passed judgment thus. It is easy for Me is either another part of the direct speech, or it is narrative.

2) (The clause), … your Lord says is addressed to the Prophet , not to Zachariah.

(19:10) He said: My Lord! give me a sign. He said: Your sign is that you will not be able to speak to the people three nights while in sound health.

As mentioned above in the narrative from Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān (3:37-41), the glad tidings came to Zachariah through the medium of the Angels who then called to him as he stood praying in the sanctuary: That God gives you the good news of John. Zachariah asked for a distinguishing sign that would separate truth from falsehood and to confirm that the call he heard was an Angelic revelation and not a satanic inception. For this reason, he received a divine distinguishing sign to which Satan had no control—knowing that Prophets are already granted divine immunity such that Satan can have no control over them.

He said: My Lord! give me a sign is a request for a distinguishing sign. God’s response was: your sign is that you will not be able to speak to the people three nights while in sound health. Hence, his tongue will be restrained

from uttering anything except for the remembrance of God , all while he will be sawiyy, that is, in sound health without any sickness or ailment. Here, not speaking to the people means not being able to speak to them. This is like saying the consequence (lāzim) [which in this case is ‘not speaking’], but meaning, metonymically, the antecedent (malzūm) [which in this case is ‘not being able to speak’]. Three nights means three nights along with their days, which is common usage. He remembered God with a variety of remembrance (dhikr), but was only able to communicate with people using sign language and gestures. Proof of all that

is in His words telling the story in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān: He said: My Lord! appoint a sign for me. He [God] said: Your sign is that you should not speak to men for three days except by signs; and remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning (3:41).

(19:11) So he went forth to his people from his place of worship (al-miḥrāb), then he made known to them (fa awḥā ilayhim) that they should glorify (God) morning and evening.

Majmaʿ al-bayān says: A miḥrāb is so-called because someone who is turned toward it in his supplication is like someone combating (muḥārib) the Devil over his prayer. The etymological origin is the council of nobles which is a forum in which each person fends for the interests of his family and kinsmen. ’Awḥā is a past tense verb that shares the same root with Īḥāʾ which means communicating something meaningful secretly and quickly. The etymological origin is captured in the saying: al-Waḥyā! al-Waḥyā! which means: Hurry! Hurry!

With this, the meaning of the verse is clear.

(19:12-13) O John! take hold of the Book with strength, and We granted him wisdom (ḥukm) while yet a child. And tenderness from Us and an increase …

There is repeated reference in His words to taking hold of the Book with strength and the commandment to do so as in: … so take hold of them with firmness and enjoin your people to take hold of what is best thereof …

(7:145); … Take hold of the law (Torah) We have given you with firmness and bear in mind what is in it … (2:63) and … Take hold of what We have given you with firmness and be obedient (2:93).

There are other verses that also have this idea. Their context bring to mind that taking hold of the Book with firmness means becoming one with its knowledge and sciences and acting in accordance with its laws, diligently and conscientiously.

Part of the verse is implied whereas the other part is kept short, all for the purpose of brevity. The implied meaning is: “When We granted him John, We told him: John, take the Book firmly both with regard to knowledge and deed”. Based on this interpretation, it is reasonable to take ‘the Book’ as the Torah1 or, alternatively, the Torah along with all of the other Prophets’ Books, because the Book which contained the code of religious law (sharīʿa) at that time was the Torah.

… and We granted him wisdom(ḥukm) while yet a child and tenderness from Us and an increase … : The word ḥukm has been interpreted as

understanding, intellect, wisdom, knowledge of the etiquette of service, true discernment, and Prophethood. However, ḥukm does not mean Prophethood as can be inferred from verses such as: And certainly We gave the Book and the wisdom (al-ḥukm) and the Prophethood to the children of Israel … (45:16) These are they to whom We gave the Book and the wisdom and the Prophethood … (6:89)

Other verses also show that ḥukm does not mean Prophethood. The same applies to interpreting it as knowledge of the etiquette of service, true discernment or intellect because there is no evidence to support any of these interpretations from the literal form of the word (lafz) or from its inferred meaning (maʿnā). It may be reminiscent of verses such as the following: … who shall recite to them Your communications and teach them the Book and the wisdom (al-ḥikma), and purify them (2:129); and … who recites to them His communications and purifies them, and teaches them the Book and the wisdom (al-ḥikma) (62:2).

In terms of construction, ḥikma (wisdom) is a type of ḥukm. Ḥukm

means knowledge of true, divine gnosis/sciences (maʿārif) and revealing that which is not disclosed to normal perception. This may be the reason why ḥukm is interpreted as understanding.

Based on the above, the meaning is: “Verily, We gave him knowledge of true sciences (maʿārifihaqīqiyya) while he was still a child, before he had even reached puberty (ḥulm)”.

The words, And tenderness from Us are linked by the conjunction “and” to the predicate, granted him wisdom while yet a child. The meaning thus rendered is: “And We granted him tenderness from Us”. Ḥanān means compassion and sympathy.

Al-Rāghib says: Because sympathy never separates from mercy (raḥmah) it is referred to as ḥanān in His Words, And tenderness from Us. Other examples are the Names of God, al-Ḥannān al-Mannān (The Tender, the Benefactor). Ḥanānik means, sympathy after sympathy [coming from You].

Ḥanān has been interpreted in several ways including that:

1) It is mercy meaning Prophethood or guardianship, as in Noah’s words: … and He has granted me mercy from Himself (11:28) and Ṣāliḥ’s words: … and He has granted to me mercy from Himself (11:63).

2) It is love. It may mean people’s love for him, as in: … and I cast down upon you love (maḥabba) from Me (20:39), meaning no one would see him without loving him.

3) It is his being compassionate, merciful, and gentle with people. He was kind to them and would advise them sincerely, guide them to God, and tell them to repent. That is why he is called John (Yuḥanna) the Baptist in the New Testament.

4) It is God’s love for him—whenever he called his Lord, according to oral tradition, God would answer him. This proves that God had special love for him, as also evidenced by the use of ḥanān in the indefinite.

Tenderness (ḥanān) being qualified as “from Us”, which is only used when characterizing what transcends and goes beyond normal or natural causes, tells us that it means a unique, divine, unprecedented kind of

fondness and affinity between him and his Lord. Thus the second and third interpretations are refuted.

Next, it is followed up with zakātan. The root meaning of the word is sound incorrupt growth. It does not fit in well with the first interpretation. Therefore, either this segment of the verse is referring to God’s love

and special care for Zachariah upon which he grew and was nurtured, or it means the love and affinity Zachariah had for his Lord and upon which he grew. Here, the growth is the growth of the soul (rūḥ). Thus, the weakness of the following claims becomes manifest:

1) zakāt means blessing—in the sense of his being blessed, helpful, and a teacher of good;

2) zakāt means charity, that is, We granted him wisdom during his formation as a charity to the people; or, it is charity from God to John’s parents, or, the wisdom given is charity from God to him; and 3) zakāt means being free of sins.

(19:13-14)… and he was one who guarded(against evil),and dutiful to his parents, and he was not insolent, disobedient.

Taqiyy is an adjective derived from taqwā, coming from the root word waqaya which has the vowel waw as its first letter (mithāl wāwī). Taqwā means guarding against what God has forbidden and avoiding forbidden acts which lead to punishment by God. Barr is an adjective derived from birr which means excellence in deeds (ʾiḥsān).

Majmaʿ al-bayān says: “Someone who is jabbār is someone who believes that no one else has any right over him, who has conceit and haughtiness. Jabbār is said of part of a date palm which is beyond one’s reach”. It can be interpreted as arrogant or haughty, and is said of someone who makes people put up with whatever he wants but someone who is unwilling to put up with anything from them. This interpretation is supported by its being followed by ʿaṣiyy which is an adjective derived from

ʿiṣyān the root meaning of which is defiance.

It is clear that the three descriptive segments in the verse explain how he was with his Creator and with creation. And he was one who guarded (against evil)—explains how he was with his with his Lord. And dutiful to his parents—explains how he was with his parents. And he was not insolent, disobedient—explains how he was with everyone else. He was kind and compassionate with people, advising them sincerely, humbly, helping the weak among them and guiding those who sought guidance. It is also clear that the claim by some that ʿaṣiyyan means disobedient to his Lord is not correct.

(19:15) And peace on him on the day he was born, and on the day he dies, and on the day he is raised to life.

The word salām (peace) means almost the same as ʾamn (safety). It appears from respective usages that the difference between the two is that ʾamn means that the locus is free of what a person hates and fears, whereas salām refers to the locus’ being such that everything a person finds in it suits him without his disliking or fearing it.

Salāmun is in the indefinite to indicate magnificence, that is, magnif cent peace will be upon him from what he would dislike on those three

days. Each of these days is the start of one of the worlds which Mankind enters and lives in. Peace will be upon him the day he is born, that is, no unpleasantness which would interfere with his happiness will touch him. Peace will be upon him on the day he dies—he will live a blissful life in the barzakh. Peace will be upon him the day he is raised to life—he will live truly there without weariness or exhaustion.

It is claimed that the added qualifier ḥayyan, which means alive, implies that he will be martyred. This is because of what God says about martyrs: … nay, they are alive [and] are provided sustenance from their Lord (3:169).

Note that the use of different tenses in “he was born, “he dies” and “he is raised” informs that the greetings of peace would be said to him during the course of his eternal life time.

God describes him in His words as a Prophet and recipient of revelation. He dubbed him with servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah) at the beginning of

His Life Story

Nothing is said about his life in the Qur’an apart from his supplication asking for a child, the answer to his supplication, and his being granted John. That was after he had seen what he had seen of Mary’s worship and favor in the sight of God.

At that point, Zachariah prayed to his Lord, asking Him to grant him good offspring from his wife even though he was a very old man and his wife was barren. His supplication was answered and the Angels called him while he was standing praying in the sanctuary: “O Zachariah! surely God gives you good news of a boy whose name shall be John”. He then asked his Lord for a sign to reassure him that the call was from Him . He was told: “Your sign will be that your tongue will be restrained making you only able to communicate with people with sign language for three days”. That is how it was—he went out of the prayer niche to his people and signaled to them to glorify morning and evening. God healed his wife for him and she bore him John (vide 3:37–41, 19:2–11, and 21:89–90).

The Qur’an did not say what happened to him or how passed away.

However, there are many oral traditions narrated by both Sunnis and Shia stating that his people killed him. His enemies went to kill him but he escaped from them and sought refuge in a tree. It opened up for him and he went right inside it. It then closed up around him. Thereafter, Satan showed the people where he was and told them to use a saw to cut down the tree. They cut it in half and he was killed.

Some oral traditions say that he was killed because the people accused him of being with Mary and making her pregnant with Christ. They said: He alone would visit her regularly. Other accounts are given.

The Story of John in the Qur’an

1. Praise for him

God makes reference to him in a few places and praises him well. He describes John as being confirmer of a Word of God, in reference to his support and confirmation of the Prophethood of Jesus. He was a leader over his people. He was chaste, and did not approach women. He was a Prophet and among the righteous (vide 3:39). He was one of the chosen ones (mujtabīn), that is, the select elite (mukhlaṣīn). He was of those who are rightly guided (mahdīyyīn) (vide 6:85–87). It was God who named him John (Yaḥyā), made him unique in his name and his person, told him to take hold of the Book with strength, granted him wisdom while yet a child, and sent peace on him the day he was born, the day he died, and the day he will be raised to life. (vide 19:2–15). He praises Zachariah’s household saying: Surely they used to hasten, one with another in deeds of goodness and to call upon Us, hoping and fearing and they were humble before Us (21:90)

“They” refers to John, his father, and his mother.

2. His Life Story

John was born miraculously to his parents—his father being a very old man and his mother barren. God granted them John when they had given up on having children [through natural means]. He became rightly guided, worshiped God and remained aloof from the material world at an early age. God granted him wisdom when he was still a child. He focused himself solely upon rites of worship, asceticism, complete devotion [to God]. He never married and was not distracted by any of the pleasures of this world (duniyā).

He was a contemporary of Jesus son of Mary and believed in his [Jesus’] Prophethood. He was a leader among his people, whose hearts felt tenderness for him and whose souls inclined toward him. People would gather round him, and until [the time] he was martyred, he would warn them, call them to repent and tell them to be God-fearing.

The account of how he was killed does not appear in the Qur’an. The oral traditions say that the Israelite king was seduced by a prostitute. W hen he visited her, John chastised him and admonished him for this. He was honored by the king who obeyed his commandments and listened to what he said. The woman then harbored enmity for him, and asked the king for John’s head and harassed him until he ordered John’s death; his throat was cut and his head was presented to her as a gif .

Some oral traditions say that it was the king’s niece who asked him for John’s head. [Some traditions state that the king] wanted to marry her but John told him not to. Her mother then made her over to captivate the king’s heart. She [the mother] sent her a note prompting her to ask for John’s head if the king granted her a wish. She did so and so John’s throat was cut and his head was placed in a golden bowl and given to her as a gif . There are many anecdotes about [John’s] asceticism, devotion and weeping out of reverend fear (khashyah) of God as well as his admonitions and wise sayings.
